posts.title: Job photo — curved radiator, bay window
posts.caption:
A curved radiator, fitted to follow the bay.

Bay windows are the coldest wall in most Bolton front rooms, and the usual answer is a flat radiator stuck on the wall next to them doing half a job.

A curved one goes where the cold actually comes in. Same heat, right place, and the room stops having a cold end.

Got a bay with nothing under it? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — service sticker
posts.caption:
This sticker is the last thing I do on a service.

Date, next due, my number. It goes on the boiler so nobody has to dig through a drawer for a certificate in twelve months' time.

Go and look at yours now. If there's no sticker, no date, and you can't remember — that's your answer.

When was yours last done? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — expansion vessel
posts.caption:
Boiler pressure keeps dropping, you keep topping it up, and there's no leak anywhere. Nine times out of ten it's this.

That's the expansion vessel. It's a cushion of air behind a rubber diaphragm, and the air slowly goes. When it's gone the pressure swings about and the safety valve dumps water outside.

It's a recharge, not a new boiler. Ten minutes with a pump and a gauge, and I check it on every service.

Topping yours up more than once a month? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — drain with roots in it
posts.caption:
A drain dug out for repair. This one had tree roots in it.

Roots find the joints in old clay pipework, get in, and grow. First it's a slow sink. Then it's a gully that fills up every time it rains. Then it's this.

The fix is to dig, cut the damaged run out, and put new pipe in with proper joints. Rodding it clears it for a month; it doesn't fix it.

Gully outside filling up in the rain? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — Ideal combi service
posts.caption:
Saturday job: an Ideal combi in for its annual service.

This is the time of year to have it done. The heating's about to go on properly, and a fault that's been sat there all summer shows up in the first cold week — when everybody else is ringing too.

A service now is a quiet half hour. The same fault in November is a cold house and a wait.

Is yours booked? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — boiler data plate
posts.caption:
Sunday tip: find this plate on your boiler and take a photo of it.

It's on the boiler somewhere — inside the front panel, behind a flap, or on the side. The GC number on it tells an engineer exactly what you've got, so when you ring with a fault I can turn up with the right part instead of coming out twice.

Thirty seconds now saves a second visit later.

Found yours? 👇

posts.title: Job photo — Greenstar Heatstore
posts.caption:
Not every boiler is a combi. This is a Worcester Greenstar Heatstore — a boiler with its own hot water store built in.

They're less common, and I've had people told "we don't do those" on the phone. They're a boiler like any other: Gas Safe engineer, manufacturer's instructions, the right parts.

If yours is a bit unusual, that's not a reason to put the service off.

What have you got on the wall? 👇

posts.title: BWD — the light one: stopcock
posts.caption:
The stopcock is always behind the one cupboard you can't get to.

Under the sink behind the bleach. In the cellar behind the Christmas decorations. In one Bolton terrace, under a floorboard in the hall with a carpet over it, which the owner found out about during a leak.

Find yours this week. Check it actually turns, because they seize over the years and a tap you can't shut off in a hurry isn't much of a stopcock. Then tell everyone in the house where it is.

Where's yours hiding?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — photo-led: autumn walk round
posts.caption:
Ten minutes outside this weekend, before the weather turns properly.

Gutters. Blocked ones spill straight down the wall every time it rains, and that wall doesn't get a chance to dry out all winter.

The gully by the back door. Leaves sat in it means water backing up across the yard in heavy rain.

Airbricks. Clear of soil, leaves, shrubs and anything stacked against the wall. They feed air to the underfloor space and, in a lot of houses, to a gas appliance.

Any overflow pipe. If one's dripping, something inside is filling past its stop point — and in a hard freeze that pipe can ice up and back the water into the loft.

None of it costs anything. All of it is cheaper than the thing it prevents.

What's the state of your gutters?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962
